extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO/OED, patent attorneys, disciplinary counsel, and respondents in PTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural/legal criteria governing investigations, proof, statute of limitations, evaluation of misconduct, and sanctions in disciplinary proceedings before the USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED). Useful for patent practitioners and counsel involved in PTO discipline cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO authority to regulate practice and impose discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress authorized the PTO to promulgate regulations governing recognition and conduct of agents, attorneys, or other persons representing applicants or other parties before the Office (35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D)). If an attorney does not comply with those regulations, or is shown to be incompetent, disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct, the PTO may suspend or exclude the attorney from further practice before the PTO (35 U.S.C. § 32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO has exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admitting persons to practice before it, and to suspend or exclude them (citing Kroll v. Finnerty and Sheinbein). This is the statutory foundation for disciplinary proceedings and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of PTO Code (Part 10) vs PTO Rules (Part 11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the PTO Code (37 C.F.R. Part 10) or the PTO Rules (37 C.F.R. Part 11) applies depends on the date of the alleged violation: Part 10 applies to conduct prior to May 3, 2013; Part 11 applies thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Part 11 Rules replaced Part 10 in 2013 and were fashioned on the ABA Model Rules. The substantive language of many charged sections remained the same; citations in decisions may reference code or rule generically unless a particular year is at issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO Code is mandatory minimum standard of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO Code is 'mandatory in character and states the minimum level of conduct below which no practitioner can fall without being subjected to disciplinary action.' (37 C.F.R. § 10.20(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO Rules carry forward that mandatory standard. Practitioners must meet at least this minimum level of conduct to avoid discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director must prove alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.49; 37 C.F.R. § 10.149). Likewise, Respondent bears the burden to prove affirmative defenses by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'clear and convincing' standard is higher than a preponderance of the evidence but lower than beyond a reasonable doubt; evidence must produce a firm belief or conviction in the trier of fact and be certain, unambiguous, and persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and start of statute-of-limitations for PTO disciplinary complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: A PTO disciplinary proceeding must be 'commenced not later than . . . 1 year after the date on which the misconduct forming the basis for the proceeding is made known to an officer or employee of the [PTO] as prescribed in the regulations' (35 U.S.C. § 32). The regulations provide that 'a complaint shall be filed within one year after the date on which the OED Director receives a grievance forming the basis of the complaint' (37 C.F.R. § 11.34(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The operative trigger is the date the OED Director receives a 'grievance' (see next criterion). The date the OED opens an investigation or dockets a matter internally depends on receipt of that grievance and controls internal statute-of-limitations calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'grievance' for initiating investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'grievance' is defined by regulation as 'a written submission from any source received by the OED Director that presents possible grounds for discipline of a specified practitioner' (37 C.F.R. § 11.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only a written submission received by the OED Director qualifies; constructive notice (e.g., public publication) or oral, undocumented contacts generally do not start the limitations period. The OED's receipt of a written grievance is the event that triggers the one-year filing period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written submission requirement — publications and informal notice insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules require a written submission received by the OED Director to initiate a disciplinary investigation; public notices or publications do not satisfy that requirement absent evidence they were submitted to and received by OED.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if disciplinary actions are published in state bulletins or other public media, the PTO regulations do not treat publication alone as receipt of a written grievance by the OED Director.

rubrics_metrics.name: No centralized interjurisdictional reporting — reliance on voluntary reporting or inter-bar contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no centralized, multi-jurisdictional database in which disciplinary information about attorneys is collected for the PTO; the PTO relies on practitioners to voluntarily inform them when they have been disciplined and on other jurisdictions to contact OED when they discipline PTO practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners are generally not required to report administrative suspensions to the PTO; state bars and other jurisdictions may or may not contact the PTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED docketing/opening date and internal record searches relevant to limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Within OED, the statute-of-limitations is tracked based on the date the investigation is opened; searches of OED records and docketing systems are used to determine whether any written grievance was received prior to a given date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal orders can compel OED to search for and produce written or oral communications that could serve as a grievance; absence of records showing prior receipt supports conclusion the limitations period began on the date of the first written submission OED received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of evidence — credibility determinations and testimonial weight
rubrics_metrics.description: The tribunal assesses witness credibility and weighs documentary and testimonial evidence in applying the clear-and-convincing standard. Direct testimony, deposition transcripts, and admitted exhibits form the record for findings of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credibility findings (e.g., finding a witness credible that she first contacted OED on a particular date) are central to resolving timing and fact disputes; lack of corroborating evidence weakens speculative claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized practice of law / pro hac vice requirements as basis for discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Practicing in a jurisdiction where one is not admitted, or appearing without required pro hac vice admission, can violate rules (e.g., Rule 5.5) and form the basis for disciplinary counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated unauthorized practice after warnings from courts is an aggravating factor and may support suspension or other sanctions; courts have authority to revoke pro hac vice admission and strike filings made by unauthorized practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for assessing sanction under 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctioning decisions consider the factors identified in 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b), including nature and seriousness of the misconduct, whether it involved dishonesty, fraud, or deceit, the extent of harm to clients or the public, whether the misconduct was willful, pattern and multiplicity of violations, prior disciplinary history, and any mitigating circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal applies § 11.54(b) factors holistically; case law and prior PTO decisions inform appropriate ranges (suspension, disbarment, etc.). The decision cites precedent holding that continuous, serious violations over time justify substantial suspension or disbarment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willfulness / intent to violate disciplinary rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Willful misconduct — deliberate or intentional disregard of rules — aggravates discipline. A practitioner’s assertion that conduct was legally justified generally does not excuse willful violations when courts have warned the practitioner and they continued conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal examines whether practitioner consciously intended the acts; even if the respondent claims a good-faith legal belief, repeated warnings and deliberate continuation support a finding of willfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of client harm as aggravating factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual injury to clients (e.g., cases dismissed, inability to obtain relief, clients left to proceed pro se, lost filing fees) is a significant aggravating factor when assessing discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific case outcomes (dismissals, loss of representation) are weighed heavily; client satisfaction alone does not negate the existence or seriousness of harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern of misconduct and repetition across jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: A demonstrated pattern of similar misconduct over multiple years and in multiple jurisdictions increases the severity of sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple violations and repeated misconduct suggest inability or unwillingness to conform to rules and indicate risk of future violations, justifying longer suspensions or disbarment.

rubrics_metrics.name: False statements, submission of false evidence, and deception during disciplinary process
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting false evidence or making false statements in the disciplinary process is an aggravating factor. If intent to deceive cannot be proven, misstatements may be treated as negligent but still aggravating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tribunal distinguishes between intentional deception (more severe) and negligent/untruthful conduct (less severe but still harmful). Credibility findings inform whether statements were intentionally deceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to acknowledge wrongdoing / lack of remorse
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner's continued insistence that their conduct was proper and failure to recognize the seriousness of misconduct is aggravating and indicates potential for future misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of remorse weighs against mitigation and supports a more severe sanction because it undermines prospects for rehabilitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooperation with investigation and litigation conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooperation with OED's investigation (timely, complete responses to requests for information) is a mitigating factor; obstruction, delays, failure to respond timely, and filing meritless or dilatory motions are aggravating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated untimely filings, excessive motions without merit, evasive responses, and stalling tactics reduce mitigation and can itself be considered misconduct reflecting poor professional behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors that may reduce sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevant mitigating factors include absence of prior disciplinary proceedings, pro bono service or good-faith motive to help underserved clients, limited assets (affecting restitution possibilities), and any other credible evidence of remorse or rehabilitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigating factors are evaluated but may be outweighed by aggravating circumstances such as repeated violations, client harm, deception, and lack of cooperation. The tribunal weighs mitigation against § 11.54(b) factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirements for appeals and post-suspension duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals from an Initial Decision under 35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. § 11.54 must be filed within 30 days with the PTO in accordance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.55 and include exceptions and supporting reasons. Suspended practitioners have duties under 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 and may petition for reinstatement per 37 C.F.R. § 11.60.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to timely appeal is deemed acceptance of the Initial Decision and waiver of further administrative and judicial review. Suspended practitioners must comply with notification and other duties set out in the rules and may seek reinstatement by following § 11.60 procedures.
